source: Booth, Bhasin, Reid, Ramani (2015) Empirical studies of functional decomposition in early design (IDETC DETC2015-47865)
finding: Study 1: novice teams used top-down, energy-flow or enumeration decomposition before concept generation. Method changed how many functions and features appeared, but most outcome measures did not differ.
numbers: 25 teams. ANOVA alpha 0.05: number of functions p=0.037, features p=0.027, unmapped features p=0.003, unmapped-feature rate p=0.001. All other metrics not significant.
limits: Small n; the authors say it was smaller than desired. Counts in their Tukey table (11, 13, 16 and 4, 12, 9) differ by metric and do not sum to 25, so the per-group n is unclear. Only decomposition and ideation phases observed. Novices only.
agent_relevance: Method choice matters at the margin only; do not expect large gains from picking one decomposition style over another.

source: Booth, Bhasin, Reid, Ramani (2015) Empirical studies of functional decomposition in early design (IDETC DETC2015-47865)
finding: Enumeration (free listing of functions) was the weakest method. Top-down produced the most functions; energy-flow produced the most final-concept features.
numbers: Mean functions: top-down 19.7, energy-flow 16.3, enumeration 15.1 (top-down > enumeration; energy-flow not separable). Mean features in final concept: energy-flow 8.8, top-down 7.4, enumeration 5.0 (energy-flow > enumeration; top-down not separable).
quote: We would recommend not using an enumeration approach for early design.
limits: Energy-flow teams added only 1.3 unmapped features on average, so the authors doubt the feature difference matters in practice. Top-down vs energy-flow called 'tenuous'.
agent_relevance: If O3 decomposes, use a structured pass (top-down or flow), not a free list. Authors advise against enumeration.

source: Booth, Bhasin, Reid, Ramani (2015) Empirical studies of functional decomposition in early design (IDETC DETC2015-47865)
finding: Study 2: among industry engineers, using functional decomposition did not correlate with design grade, overall or on any rubric part.
numbers: 78 reports from an online graduate course (low-cost clothes washer, individual work). 51% used some form of decomposition. Correlation with total grade r=0.075, p=0.515. Same for every rubric subcategory. Graded by at least two instructors, normalised; 100 points, feasibility worth 40.
limits: Correlational, not randomised. Method was optional and only listed as an example. Use coded as yes or no; quality judged separately. Decomposition was a named example in the rubric for the ideation item, so grader bias against it is unlikely.
agent_relevance: Having a decomposition step in the scaffold is not evidence of better answers. O3 needs its own measured test before it earns a place.

source: Booth, Bhasin, Reid, Ramani (2015) Empirical studies of functional decomposition in early design (IDETC DETC2015-47865)
finding: Most engineer function diagrams were poor, which may explain the null. Many contained non-functions (needs, parts).
numbers: 51% of function diagrams rated very low quality. Mean 14.4 functions (SD 9.0). Mean 5.88 syntax errors per diagram (SD 6.0). Hierarchy diagrams most common (44% in Fig 1, 34.6% in text); plain function tree 29.27%; energy-flow diagrams least common.
limits: Quality rated by the authors; the figure and text percentages for diagram types disagree. Cannot separate 'method does not work' from 'method used badly'.
agent_relevance: Decomposition quality is the moderator. Add a code check that each sub-function is a verb-noun transformation, not a part or a need.

source: Booth, Bhasin, Reid, Ramani (2015) Empirical studies of functional decomposition in early design (IDETC DETC2015-47865)
finding: A different method, the morphological matrix, did weakly predict grade in the same sample where decomposition did not.
numbers: Matrix use vs total grade r=0.233, p=0.040; vs ideation grade r=0.293, p=0.009. Syntax errors vs 'identify needs' grade r=0.222, p=0.050; syntax errors vs matrix use r=-0.247, p=0.029.
limits: Weak correlations, many tests, no correction stated. Observational.
agent_relevance: The step after decomposition (combining sub-solutions into concepts) may carry the benefit. Test O3 plus a combine step against O3 alone.

source: Booth, Bhasin, Reid, Ramani (2015) Empirical studies of functional decomposition in early design (IDETC DETC2015-47865)
finding: Functions from the diagram persisted into the final concept. The function list seems to fix the design space.
numbers: Nearly all final-concept features mapped to a function; not all functions mapped to features. Unmapped features per team: energy-flow 1.3, enumeration 0.2, top-down 0.0.
limits: Authors give three readings: decomposition defines the space, scope was fixed before decomposing (fixation), or the mental model does not mature. Data cannot separate them. Earlier and later phases not observed.
agent_relevance: Risk for O3: a wrong or narrow first decomposition bounds all later search. Keep a rule to re-decompose after a failed check (G1).

source: Booth, Reid, Ramani (2013) Understanding abstraction in design: comparison of three functional analysis methods for product dissection (DETC2013-13130)
finding: Within-subject comparison of three analysis methods for dissection found no difference, statistical or practical.
numbers: 26 mechanical engineering students, 3 conditions (top-down, energy-flow, unstructured), n=78 trees, devices: hair dryer, power drill, NERF pistol. No significant method effect on number of functions, errors, levels of abstraction, unique subsystems or functions. Hypotheses H1 to H4 all rejected.
limits: Reverse engineering of existing products, not new design. Task may be too simple. Device order is confounded with time. Semi-random sample. No effect size reported because n<100. A null does not prove equivalence.
agent_relevance: For analysis of a known thing, a structured decomposition prompt may add nothing over free description. Test before adding.

source: Booth, Reid, Ramani (2013) Understanding abstraction in design: comparison of three functional analysis methods for product dissection (DETC2013-13130)
finding: Covariates mattered more than method: class level, device, prior device experience, and fatigue.
numbers: Levels of abstraction rose with class level (sophomore 3.5, junior 4.17, senior 4.84). Functions per tree fell over the three rounds (device effect on total functions F=3.63, p=0.0352). Prior experience with a device raised errors (F=3.90, p=0.055). 14 of 26 said they had never learned functional decomposition, though it is required in sophomore design.
limits: Time and device are confounded. Recall of prior teaching is self-report.
agent_relevance: Skill and fatigue effects: repeated forced decomposition may degrade. Budget one decomposition per problem.

source: Booth, Reid, Ramani (2013) Understanding abstraction in design: comparison of three functional analysis methods for product dissection (DETC2013-13130)
finding: Observed failure modes of novices: confusing parts with functions, finding flows hard, stopping at a general level when top-down.
numbers: Qualitative notes: energy-flow was hard because flows are not obvious and do not fit a tree; top-down users stayed general because they felt they had the gist; many conflated parts and functions despite emphasis in the instructions; electrical functions mostly missed.
limits: Observation by the authors, no counts.
agent_relevance: The same errors are likely in LLM output: parts named as functions, stopping early. Both are checkable in code.

source: Linsey, Green, Van Wie, Wood, Stone (2005) Functional representations in conceptual design: a first study in experimental design and evaluation (ASEE)
finding: First controlled test of whether giving a function list helps concept generation. Preliminary result: no difference from control.
numbers: 54 senior design-methods students, random assignment to control (no technique) or functions group (given a function set), 45 minutes, 'art enabling device' problem. Mean ideas: control 19.0 (SD 8.6, n=5), functions 19.7 (SD 5.8, n=7). Mean concept novelty: control 2.22 (SD 0.23, n=11), functions 2.16 (SD 0.43, n=13).
quote: functional modeling ... is indistinguishable from the experimental control and does not inhibit the idea generation process
limits: Preliminary analysis of one session; tiny cells; novelty scored by one author. Authors say the result does not settle the hypothesis. The functions group was handed the functions, so it tests a given function list, not the act of decomposing.
agent_relevance: A given function list did not raise idea count. Do not assume O3 raises variety.

source: Linsey, Green, Van Wie, Wood, Stone (2005) Functional representations in conceptual design: a first study in experimental design and evaluation (ASEE)
finding: Control group made more highly novel concepts. Authors suggest decomposition pulls toward concrete, narrower solutions.
numbers: Concepts scoring 4 or more on novelty: control 5, functions 2 (7 total). Scores 3 or more: control 26, functions 23. Control produced 71% of the concepts in the top half of the scale.
limits: Counts are small and raw, no test reported. Novelty rated by one author.
agent_relevance: Possible cost of decomposing first: less novelty. For problems needing novelty, test generating before decomposing.

source: Atilola, Tomko, Linsey (2016) The effects of representation on idea generation and design fixation: sketches versus function trees (Design Studies)
finding: Reported in secondary summaries only: showing a function tree as the example did not cause fixation versus control, and caused less fixation than showing a sketch.
numbers: Direction only; participant counts and effect sizes were NOT read.
limits: Not opened. Cannot verify numbers or task. Treat as unverified until the paper is read.
agent_relevance: Function-level hints may be safer than concrete examples when the agent is shown a prior solution. Verify first.

source: Clemson dissertation (n.d.) Function models, interaction models and pruned function models for concept generation
finding: The abstract says pruned function models (solution detail removed) are easier to understand and gave better concepts than standard function models. It also says there is little experimental evidence that function models help ideation.
numbers: Abstract only; no numbers on the page. Three studies: designer understanding, a computational similarity metric for abstraction level, and concept generation.
limits: Only the abstract was read; sample sizes and effects unknown. Author name and year not shown on the page; year approximate.
agent_relevance: Keep sub-functions solution-neutral. Strip implementation words from each sub-function before using it to prompt generation.

source: Exploring the impact of functional terms on idea generation in design (CIE 2018)
finding: Functional terms used as stimuli raised usefulness, novelty and variety of ideas in novices, with no sign of fixation.
numbers: 20 novice student designers. Significant gains on usefulness, novelty and variety (no statistics on the page).
limits: Abstract only. No control group, task or test details visible. Small n. Direction differs from the 2005 null, so effect may depend on how functions are used (stimuli versus a fixed list).
agent_relevance: Use function words as prompts for varied ideation, not only as a fixed checklist.

source: Van Eck, McAdams, Vermaas (2007) Functional decomposition: three models of functional reasoning compared (DETC2007)
finding: A survey of Functional Basis, Function-Behavior-State and Functional Reasoning finds that the models differ in how they represent function and how they decompose, with no consensus view.
numbers: No numbers. Three models compared on function representation and decomposition strategy.
limits: Abstract only. Conceptual comparison; no test of which works better.
agent_relevance: There is no single canonical decomposition. Fix one form for the agent (for example verb-noun with flows) and test it.

source: Massoudi and Fuge (2025) Agentic LLMs for conceptual systems engineering and design (arXiv 2507.08619)
finding: A nine-agent system and a two-agent generator-reflector loop were compared on requirements extraction, functional decomposition and simulator code for a solar water filter. Requirement coverage stayed near zero for both.
numbers: 60 runs: 2 LLMs (Llama 3.3 70B, DeepSeek R1 70B) x 2 systems x 3 temperatures x 5 seeds. JSON validity 100% in all. Requirement coverage 0% in nearly all cells; best 20% (R1, multi-agent, T=0.0). Embodiment tagging 100%.
limits: One case study, small local models, coverage judged by their own metric. No human baseline.
agent_relevance: LLM decomposition gave valid structure but missed most requirements. Add a code check that every requirement maps to at least one sub-function.

source: Massoudi and Fuge (2025) Agentic LLMs for conceptual systems engineering and design (arXiv 2507.08619)
finding: More agents gave finer decomposition at higher cost and with crashes. The simple two-agent loop with the reasoning model collapsed to one node.
numbers: DeepSeek R1 70B: multi-agent 5 to 6 nodes (6.0 +/- 1.9 at T=1.0), about 650 s; two-agent 1 node at T=0.0 in 38.6 s. Code executability: Llama two-agent 94.7% at T=0.5, Llama multi-agent 40 to 49%; R1 two-agent 100% at T=0.0 (1 node). Llama multi-agent crashed (over 60,000 tokens or recursion limit 30).
limits: Node count is not quality; extra nodes may be duplicates. Temperature differences noisy (SD up to 28 points on 5 seeds).
agent_relevance: Finer granularity went with less runnable code. Granularity needs a code gate, not more agents.

source: Elhambakhsh, Grandi, Ko (2025) Domain adaptation of LLMs for classifying mechanical assembly components (arXiv 2505.01627)
finding: Fine-tuning GPT-3.5 Turbo on labelled parts lifted function-class accuracy a lot over the pre-trained model, but accuracy fell as the training set grew and rare classes did poorly.
numbers: Text: pre-trained accuracy about 4% rose to about 90% with 681 training samples (10% split) of 7,568 unique parts. 99% of predicted labels fell inside the predefined classes. Table 3: train accuracy 0.93 at 10% of data down to 0.64 at 90%. Authors suspect overfitting and class imbalance.
limits: Classifies single-part function, not decomposition. Test columns in the table were not cleanly parsed. Labels from a fixed list.
agent_relevance: Labelling a part's function from a closed vocabulary works with few examples. Open decomposition is a harder, different task.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-most prompting enables complex reasoning in LLMs (ICLR)
finding: Splitting a problem into easier subproblems and solving in order gave very large gains on a length-generalisation test.
numbers: SCAN length split, code-davinci-002: least-to-most 99.7%, chain-of-thought 16.2%, standard few-shot 16.7%. text-davinci-002 (100 commands): 76.0 vs 0.0 vs 6.0. code-davinci-001: 60.7 vs 0.0 vs 0.4.
limits: Synthetic grammar with a hand-built decomposition prompt. 2022 models. Not a design task.
agent_relevance: Strong case for decomposition when sub-steps are simple and known. Weak evidence for open design problems.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-most prompting enables complex reasoning in LLMs (ICLR)
finding: On math word problems the decomposition gain was small overall but larger on long problems, and a hand-made decomposition fixed nearly every failure.
numbers: GSM8K: least-to-most 62.39% vs chain-of-thought 60.87%. By steps: 5+ steps 45.23 vs 39.07; 2 steps 74.53 vs 76.68 (decomposition worse); 3 steps 68.91 vs 67.29; 4 steps 59.73 vs 59.39. DROP numerical: non-football 82.45 vs 74.77; football 73.42 vs 59.56.
limits: Same model both arms. The model's own decomposition is the weak step, not the solving.
agent_relevance: Value lies in the quality of the split. A model-made split of an open problem is the weak link; check it. Gain depends on problem length.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve prompting (ACL)
finding: A zero-shot instruction to make a plan, then execute, improved over zero-shot chain-of-thought, mainly by cutting missing-step errors; the detailed version did best.
numbers: text-davinci-003, average over 6 arithmetic sets: CoT 70.4, PS 73.5, PS+ 76.7. GSM8K 56.4 / 57.0 / 59.3; SVAMP 69.9 / 70.8 / 75.7; AQuA 38.9 / 43.9 / 46.0. CommonsenseQA 65.2 to 71.9; StrategyQA 63.8 to 65.4; last letter 64.8 to 75.2.
limits: Gains 1 to 7 points; plain PS on GSM8K gains 0.6. Plan quality not scored. One model family.
agent_relevance: A plan step helps modestly, mostly on missing steps. Do not expect a large lift from a generic plan-first prompt.

source: Khot et al. (2023) Decomposed prompting: a modular approach for solving complex tasks (ICLR)
finding: Giving each sub-task its own prompt beat putting the whole procedure in one chain-of-thought, especially for longer inputs.
numbers: kth-letter concatenation (100 test examples per setting): decomposed prompting stays close to 100% as words increase while chain-of-thought and least-to-most drop. List reversal with davinci-001: base chain-of-thought does not generalise to longer lists; recursive decomposition does. Multi-hop QA (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue): beat the no-decomposition baseline in all settings except Codex on HotpotQA (comparable).
limits: Only trends recorded; bar values were read from a garbled figure. Tasks hand-designed to decompose cleanly.
agent_relevance: Separate calls for separate sub-tasks (as in the schema's slots) outperformed one long reasoning chain.

source: Prasad et al. (2024) ADaPT: as-needed decomposition and planning with LLMs (NAACL Findings)
finding: Decomposing only when the executor fails, recursively, beat static plan-and-execute and retry baselines on agent tasks.
numbers: ALFWorld success: ADaPT 71.6, ReAct 43.3, Plan-and-Execute 43.3, Reflexion 57.5. WebShop: ADaPT 44.0, ReAct 32.0, Plan-and-Execute 17.0, LATS 38.0. TextCraft: ADaPT 52.0, ReAct 19.0, Plan-and-Execute 27.0, Reflexion 32.0.
limits: GPT-3.5 executors, three text environments, one dataset built by the same authors. Gains cost extra calls.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G1: decompose on failure, not by schedule. Static up-front decomposition was no better than ReAct on ALFWorld and worse on WebShop (17 vs 32).

source: Prasad et al. (2024) ADaPT: as-needed decomposition and planning with LLMs (NAACL Findings)
finding: Depth and executor strength moderate the gain: deeper recipes need deeper decomposition, and a weak executor gains most.
numbers: TextCraft recipe depth 2: ReAct 26.9 to ADaPT 78.2; depth 3: 1.8 to 38.7. Weak executor (atomic skills only): 3.3 to 41.7. Improved all tested LLMs, GPT-4 by up to 37 points. Max decomposition depth actually used rose with recipe depth (1.9 at depth 2, 2.8 at depth 3).
limits: Per-depth ablation on ALFWorld not extracted. Environment is rule-based and cleanly decomposable.
agent_relevance: Cap depth; allow deeper split only after a check fails. Expect largest gains when the base solver is weak.

source: Dziri et al. (2023) Faith and fate: limits of transformers on compositionality (NeurIPS)
finding: On multi-step compositional tasks accuracy falls toward zero as the computation graph deepens, even for GPT-4; models seem to match pieces rather than reason systematically.
numbers: 3-digit by 3-digit multiplication: ChatGPT 55%, GPT-4 59%. Zero- and few-shot accuracy decays from near perfect to near zero with problem size. Fine-tuned GPT-3 did not generalise beyond the trained size.
limits: Synthetic tasks (multiplication, logic grid puzzles, dynamic programming). Error-propagation argument is theoretical.
agent_relevance: A decomposition with more steps adds places to fail. Keep step count small and verify each step with code.

source: Radhakrishnan et al. (2023) Question decomposition improves the faithfulness of model-generated reasoning (arXiv 2307.11768)
finding: Answering sub-questions in separate contexts made the stated reasoning more faithful, at some accuracy cost compared with chain-of-thought.
numbers: Average accuracy over tasks: zero-shot 72.8, few-shot 79.7, chain-of-thought 87.0, chain-of-thought decomposition 88.0, factored decomposition 81.8. With inserted mistakes the accuracy drop was: chain-of-thought 21.3, chain-of-thought decomposition 29.1, factored decomposition 9.2 points.
limits: HotpotQA, OpenBookQA, StrategyQA, TruthfulQA only; few-shot; some table cells garbled, so only averages are quoted.
agent_relevance: Separate-context sub-calls cost about 5 points of accuracy but depend less on earlier mistakes. Supports slot-filling design.

source: Gap record: LLM functional decomposition of engineering products scored against expert references
finding: Gap: no peer-reviewed study was opened that scores LLM-made function structures (Functional Basis) against expert references. The 2024 Function-Behavior-Structure prompting paper and the 2025 Monte Carlo tree-search decomposition paper (GPT-4o) were found only in search summaries and could not be opened (search quota used up; arXiv and OpenAlex rate-limited).
numbers: None.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Key evidence for O3 on engineering products is missing. Run our own test: LLM decomposition scored against a held-out reference function structure.
